newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan FTC to seek end to ban on holding companies.
newsitem.headline: Japan FTC to seek end to ban on holding companies.

text.p: Japan's anti-monopoly watchdog, the Fair Trade Commission (FTC), said on Wednesday it plans to submit a bill to parliament to abolish a longstanding ban on holding companies.
FTC officials quoted Shogo Itoda, the FTC's secretary general, as saying it will submit the bill to revise the Anti-Monopoly Law to the next ordinary session of parliament, which opens in January.

The FTC had sought to revise the law to remove the ban on holding companies earlier this year. The attempt failed due opposition from a member of the Social Democratic Party, a partner in the then-ruling coalition.
A holding company is a firm which has control of one or more other companies, often by having a majority of shares in them, but does not engage in a specific business.

Since the pro-business Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) formed a minority government under Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on November 9, senior LDP legislators have expressed a willingness to relax the ban on holding companies.
An FTC official said that while the commission wants to broadly relax the ban, details of the revision have not been discussed yet.
Separately, Hashimoto unveiled plans last month to liberalise financial markets to catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and the United States.

In line with financial reform plans, which call for banks, securities firms and insurance firms to enter each other's sectors, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) is currently discussing establishment of financial holding companies.
The most likely way to break down the wall between financial industry sectors would be to allow holding companies, a MOF official said recently.

The FTC's Itoda was quoted as saying that there was a view that financial holding firms would be free of regulations, but they would be subject to the same restrictions as other industries if they violated the Anti-Monopoly Law.
